newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Parliament seeks ways to boost TENs.
newsitem.headline: Parliament seeks ways to boost TENs.

text.p: The European Parliament is determined to secure more spending on giant European rail and road networks to boost jobs, despite opposition from EU finance ministers struggling to qualify for the single currency.

The chairman of the parliament's budget committee, German social democrat Detlev Samland, told Reuters on Thursday that all political groups in the European Union assembly favoured additional funding for trans-European networks (TENs).
Samland said the parliament would vote next week on at least one proposal on how to boost financing for the projects.
This comes after finance ministers in Luxembourg on Monday steadfastly refused to endorse a European Commission's plan to spend more than $1 billion to give a jolt to the infrastructure projects.

The 14 priority projects, identified by EU leaders at a summit in Essen in December 1994, include high-speed trains between Paris and Cologne and between Frankfurt and London, plus motorways in Greece, Spain and Portugal.
The extra 1.0 billion Ecus ($1.25 billion) would kick-start nine of the 14 projects, Commission officials say.

Samland said the parliament would at its session in Strasbourg, France, next week vote on a proposal from its Socialist group to allocate 300 million Ecus from the 1997 budget to spending on the TENs.
In addition, 100 million would go to research spending and another 100 million to help the Northern Ireland peace process.
Of these 500 million Ecus, 270 million would come from savings but the EU budget would also need to be increased.
However, the second largest group in parliament, the conservative European People's Party, was against this solution.
Samland said he would now hold political talks on a second proposal to earmark the saved 270 million Ecus for the TENs, research and Northern Ireland.
In addition, there would be a decision in principle that other savings would also go to these projects.
"We have made such savings (in the EU budget) as the parliament has never done before," he said.
Samland said both proposals were legally within the parliament's powers.
The reluctance of the ministers to approve additional funding stems from their all-out effort to meet the Maastricht treaty's tough criteria on budgets and debt for monetary union.
Any surplus funds in the EU budget are normally returned to national governments.
The road and rail networks were an integral part of Santer's confidence pact for employment, an initiative launched earlier in the year to tackle the union's mounting jobless rate.
With unemployment widely seen as the EU's most pressing problem, there is a desire within the Commission to appear responsive to the worries of the average citizen. (1$=0.80 Ecus)
